PAPER: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2026) 18:6 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-025-02358-5 RESEARCH A single test for raw material properties: hardness and stiffness of tools-stones from Sibhudu Vi Fratta1 · Nicholas J. Conard1 · Patrick Schmidt1,2 Received: 24 February 2025 / Accepted: 31 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The study of raw materials used for making stone tools allows archaeologists to gain insight into the behaviours of ancient people. Raw materials possess different properties, which influence the ability of knappers to flake, shape and use a stone tool. Measuring these properties experimentally requires specialised laboratories and measuring processes that are not straightforward. This makes such analyses a cost-intensive and often inaccessible way to investigate the past. Here, we present an alternative way to evaluate two mechanical properties, stiffness and hardness, using a single indentation test. We also test whether these two isolated measures allow making predictions on raw material selection and tool shape. We analysed tool-stones from the Middle Stone Age site Sibhudu on South Africa’s eastern seaboard. The site has yielded a rich assemblage of tools from different raw materials. We found that a single indentation test allows measuring hardness and stiffness reliably, simplifying the measurement protocol of raw material studies. We also observed weak correlations between those isolated properties and the shape of the finished tools. This has implications for future studies of Stone Age raw materials, proposing a simplified testing protocol. We also discuss the role of stiffness in stone knapping. We excluded the Sibudan from the correlation analysis because the entire layer yielded only three blades, rendering its sample size too small for analysis. Combining data from all three layers, hornfels and dol- erite, which have comparable elastic moduli, also have comparable average lengths. Quartzite pieces appear to be longer and have an E = 57.71 GPa. While in the total sample, dolerite and hornfels appear to have almost identical average lengths, in the HP, doler- ite pieces are on average smaller than the hornfels pieces. However, dolerite data strays more widely as shown by the error bars in Fig. 8. Except for sandstone, the correlation between a higher E value and a higher average length is particularly pronounced in layer Thabo. The Ilembian data set is incomplete, as it includes only 15 blades. No meaningful correlation can be observed in this assemblage. For the platform width, data from the entire sample, even when considering the degree of variation displayed by the error bars, show an inverse relationship between lithic met- rics and mechanical properties. The average width of the platform decreases as the HK and E values increase. The correlation is stronger with E (R2 = 0.97) than with HK, although the patternis not as uniform when examining the layers individually. Quartzite shows a contrasting behaviour in the HP, with the highest overall measurement, and this layer presents the lowest R2 value (R2 = 0.6325). The data set presents no discernible correlation between the attributes thickness, width and either of the two mechan- ical properties (Table 3). Hornfels blades appear to be the thinnest and narrowest on average in all layers, while sand- stone pieces are the thickest and widest, with values more akin to quartzite than dolerite and hornfels. JSON: Name: single_knoop_indentation_pipeline Title: Using a single Knoop indentation to derive hardness and stiffness for predicting toolstone selection and blade metric outcomes in lithic assemblages Short Hypothesis: Higher Young's modulus and higher Knoop hardness values obtained from a single Knoop indentation cause knappers to produce blades with greater mean length and narrower platform widths when reduction strategy and percussion type are held constant. Related Work: Existing approaches for characterizing lithic raw materials rely on multi-method mechanical testing (e.g., Vickers/Knoop hardness, three-point bending and tensile tests, fracture toughness measures) and macroscopic petrographic descriptions. Empirical relationships between indentation hardness and elastic modulus have been proposed and refined to account for elastic recovery and true contact area; these enable estimation of Young's modulus from indentation but require careful correction for indenter geometry and material response. Archaeological studies have used direct mechanical measures to link material properties to production strategies and tool types, and experimental knapping research has shown that percussion type, blank size/shape and knapper technique strongly influence blade metrics. Limitations in current practice include: (1) requirement for multiple specialized tests and equipment, increasing cost and decreasing accessibility; (2) variability and failure of indentations on heterogeneous or porous toolstones; (3) inconsistent predictive power when using isolated HK or E values without accounting for confounds (blank geometry, hammer type, heat treatment); and (4) lack of standardized pipelines combining single-indentation-derived metrics with controlled knapping experiments and statistical models to evaluate causal effects. Abstract: This pipeline formalizes a testable research workflow that uses a single Knoop indentation to derive Knoop hardness and an indentation-corrected Young’s modulus and then evaluates whether these two measures predict knapping outcomes and raw-material selection. The pipeline combines: (1) standardized single-indentation acquisition (fixed loads, imaging, corrected HK and E computation), (2) controlled knapping experiments across representative toolstones with fixed blank geometry and percussion regimes, and (3) statistical models that compare indentation-derived predictors to full-mechanical baselines and material-availability null models. The main contribution is an experimentally validated protocol and analysis plan that quantifies how much variance in blade length and platform width is explained by single-indentation HK and E under controlled conditions. Expected outcomes are (i) quantified predictive power (R2, RMSE) of HK and E alone and combined, (ii) comparison to multi-test mechanical baselines, and (iii) identification of measurement failure modes and sample conditions where single-indentation estimates are reliable or insufficient. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Archaeological sample: lithic assemblage from Sibhudu layers (Bart, Thabo, YA2i) as used in the referenced study (n≈713 artifacts); retain raw-material labels, complete blade metrics, platform width, blank dimensions, context layer. (B) Experimental knapping dataset: produce controlled blade sets for five representative raw materials (dolerite, hornfels, quartzite, hydrothermal quartz, sandstone). For each material: prepare standardized blanks (N=40 blanks per material), and produce blades under two percussion regimes (hard hammer, soft stone hammer), with two knappers of matched expert skill; target at least 200 complete blades total. Mechanical measurements: for every raw-material sample perform (1) single Knoop indentations: 100 N and 200 N loads, 15 indentations per sample, image with laser-scanning microscope, compute corrected Knoop hardness HK' and corrected Young's modulus E' using the Ben Ghorbal correction; (2) baseline full mechanical tests on matched slabs: Vickers hardness, three-point bending to get direct E, fracture toughness where feasible. Baselines: (i) null model (raw-material availability frequency predicts selection), (ii) models using only HK', (iii) models using only E', (iv) combined HK'+E', (v) combined HK'+E'+derived properties (fracture toughness, direct E). Experimental setup: align blank geometry across materials (equal length, width, thickness), control percussion (protocol scripts), randomize knapper–material assignments, record hammer type, number of strikes, and resulting blade metrics (length, width, thickness, platform width). Evaluation metrics: for continuous outcomes (blade length, platform width): adjusted R2, RMSE, MAE, regression coefficient p-values, AIC/BIC. For material selection prediction: classification accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC for models predicting material choice from blade metrics and/or indentation values. Statistical models: linear regressions, multiple regressions with covariates (blank size, hammer type, knapper as random effect), ANCOVA, mixed-effects models. Ablations/comparisons: (1) HK' only vs E' only vs HK'+E'; (2) single-indentation-derived E' vs direct three-point bending E; (3) inclusion vs exclusion of percussion type and blank size covariates; (4) effect of indentation load (100 N vs 200 N) on predictive power. Cross-validation: 5-fold cross-validation on experimental dataset; separate hold-out archaeological test set to test model transfer. Hypothesis test: predefine success criterion as combined HK'+E' explaining >50% (>0.5 adjusted R2) of variance in blade length and platform width under controlled percussion and blank-size conditions; report p-values and 95% confidence intervals. Power analysis: compute sample sizes required to detect an R2 increase from 0.2 to 0.5 at α=0.05, power=0.8 and adjust N accordingly. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement failure and noise: Knoop indentations can fail or be unreadable on heterogeneous, coarse-grained, or porous stones, and higher loads increase failure rates; surface preparation and polishing may be infeasible on archaeological artifacts. Estimation bias: corrected E' and HK' rely on assumptions (elastic recovery, contact geometry) that may not hold for anisotropic or composite rocks, producing systematic biases. Confounding variables: blade metrics depend strongly on blank geometry, hammer type, knapper skill, heat treatment, and reduction strategy; controlling these is necessary to infer causality but limits applicability to archaeological assemblages with unknown procedures. Sample size and representativeness: archaeological contexts may yield small or unbalanced samples per raw material, reducing statistical power and generalizability. Destructiveness and access: baseline full-mechanical tests and slab preparation may be destructive or require specialized permits; limited access to equipment constrains scalability. External validity: findings calibrated on a limited set of rock types and specific percussion regimes may not generalize to other regions, raw materials, or knapping traditions. Statistical limitations: observed correlations may not imply behavioral causation in archaeological contexts absent independent evidence of percussion regime and blank preparation.
